title: Brazilian Present Perfect: Tenho feito
summary: Use tenho feito to describe repeated or ongoing actions continuing into the present, not a simple past event.

sections.heading: Not the same as English present perfect
sections.body: Portuguese **tenho + past participle** usually means an action has been repeated or ongoing lately. It does **not** normally translate a single completed experience like English 'I have been to Brazil'.

examples.en: I have been studying a lot lately.
She has been working too much.

examples.pt: A gente tem comido fora toda semana.
examples.en: We have been eating out every week.

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body:
Use the present of **ter** plus the past participle: falado, comido, aberto. The participle stays masculine singular in this compound tense.

| Subject | falar | comer | abrir | fazer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| eu | **tenho falado** | **tenho comido** | **tenho aberto** | **tenho feito** |
| você/ele/ela | **tem falado** | **tem comido** | **tem aberto** | **tem feito** |
| nós | **temos falado** | **temos comido** | **temos aberto** | **temos feito** |
| vocês/eles/elas | **têm falado** | **têm comido** | **têm aberto** | **têm feito** |

examples.pt: Eu tenho falado com ele todos os dias.
examples.en: I have been speaking with him every day.
We have been receiving many messages.

sections.heading: Simple past for completed experiences
sections.body: For a completed experience or a specific past event, Portuguese usually uses the **pretérito perfeito** instead.

keyPoints: Tenho feito means repeated or ongoing action up to now.
It is not a general equivalent of English 'have done'.
The auxiliary ter agrees with the subject: tenho, tem, temos, têm.
Use simple preterite with já for life experiences.
The participle does not agree in tenho feito.

commonMistakes.wrong: Tenho ido ao Brasil uma vez.
commonMistakes.note: A single completed experience uses preterite.

commonMistakes.wrong: Eu tenho visto esse filme ontem.
